Hatchlings of the Montane woodcreeper emerge from eggs incubated at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], and the incubation period culminates in an age at hatching of 18 days [ab = 18 days]. These newly emerged young are altricial and completely dependent on parental care, weighing approximately 6.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 6.1 grams] at the moment of hatching. This initial mass is modest when compared to other members of the Dendrocolaptinae subfamily, reflecting the relatively small clutch size and the energetic constraints of montane insectivory. The nestling period proceeds rapidly under the constant brooding of both parents, who maintain the microclimate of the nest cavity. Field observations from the eastern slopes of the Peruvian Andes indicate that juveniles begin to achieve short, fluttering flights and depart from the nest cavity at 19 days after hatching [tx = 19 days after hatching], a developmental milestone that coincides with the full emergence of the rectrices and primary flight feathers at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This fledging age is relatively abbreviated for a bird of its ultimate body size, and it may represent an adaptive response to the high predation pressure characteristic of Neotropical cloud forest environments.

As the young birds transition to nutritional independence, their growth trajectory accelerates toward the adult body mass values that distinguish the sexes. Adult males of Lepidocolaptes lacrymiger reach a maximum body weight of approximately 35.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 35.4 grams], a value that places them at the upper end of the size range for the genus. Females, by contrast, attain a slightly lower asymptotic mass of about 34.6 grams [Wwi = about 34.6 grams], a difference that likely reflects subtle ecological partitioning of foraging niches rather than a pronounced sexual dimorphism in bill or body dimensions. These ultimate wet weights are consistent with the species' specialization on bark-gleaning arthropods, a foraging mode that demands a light yet robust frame for vertical climbing on moss-laden tree trunks. Some specimen series collected in the Cordillera de Mérida, Venezuela, report a female mass range of 29.5 to 33 grams, suggesting that the average mass values given here align closely with the upper bounds of the population variation observed across Andean elevations. This variation may be linked to local prey abundance and the energetic demands of thermoregulation in cooler microclimates.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Montane woodcreepers follows a predictable sequence of developmental transitions, all measured under thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic phase of this species. When maintained at a body temperature typical of sustained activity, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the gonadal development of juveniles culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid pubertal transition suggests that the species follows a fast pace-of-life strategy for a tropical passerine, allowing individuals to enter the breeding population early if environmental conditions permit. The age at first successful breeding, however, is delayed substantially beyond the onset of gametogenesis. Under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], individuals typically initiate their first brood at approximately 438 days after hatching [tR = approximately 438 days after hatching], equivalent to about 1.2 years. This interval between reaching sexual maturity and first reproduction likely reflects the time required to establish a permanent territory, secure a mate, and accumulate sufficient body condition to sustain the energetic costs of egg production and nestling provisioning in the competitive environment of the Andean forest understory.

Reproductive output in the Montane woodcreeper is modest, consistent with the life-history characteristics of many tropical insectivorous birds that occupy stable, resource-limited habitats. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and, during the breeding season, typically raise only one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year]. This low fecundity is offset by a notably extended lifespan, which maximizes the total number of reproductive opportunities over an individual's lifetime. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated at approximately 2,446 days [am = approximately 2,446 days], when measured under the standard active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Such a lifespan, while modest by the standards of larger tropical birds, is considerable for a 35-gram passerine, and it underscores a strategy of high adult survival coupled with low annual reproductive investment. The annual reproductive rate, therefore, is best characterized as one brood per year, yielding a total lifetime output of roughly 6 to 7 eggs under ideal conditions. Comparative data from closely related woodcreepers suggest that this combination of delayed first reproduction and extended adult survival is a conserved trait within the Dendrocolaptinae.

Basal metabolic demands in Lepidocolaptes lacrymiger have been quantified through flow-through respirometry on post-absorptive individuals resting during the inactive phase of their circadian cycle. At a stable ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximal rate of oxygen consumption recorded under these standard conditions reached 40 milliliters per hour [JOi = 40 milliliters per hour]. This metabolic rate is relatively low for a bird of its body mass, a pattern that aligns with the general trend among Neotropical insect-eaters inhabiting cool, hypoxic montane environments where energy conservation is at a premium. The value is comparable to those reported for other bark-foraging furnariids of similar size, and it suggests a resting metabolism that is finely tuned to the thermal neutral zone of the species. The energetic efficiency implied by this low metabolic rate likely facilitates the maintenance of body condition during the long non-breeding season, when arthropod prey may be scarce. It may also play a role in enabling the species' relatively long maximum lifespan, as lower rates of cellular oxidative metabolism are often correlated with reduced senescence and greater longevity in endotherms.
